historical_record.description: The Fine Arts Building of the California Midwinter International Exposition, designed by the architect C. C. McDougall, was built here — the first of the five building campaigns that made the museum.
The M. H. de Young Memorial Museum was built to the design of Louis Christian Mullgardt, over 1917 to 1921.
The museum was expanded by the architects Weeks and Day.
The 1894 Fine Arts Building was demolished in the course of a central expansion and interior remodelling designed by Frederick H. Meyer.
The museum's exterior was remodelled by the City Architect Dodge A. Riedy.
The museum's west wing was demolished and the Brundage Wing built in its place, to the design of Gardiner Dailey.

The City Planning Commission denied, 4-1, an appeal against the negative declaration for an elevated double access ramp, 14½ feet wide, designed by the architect Adolph Rosekrans for the museum's entrance on the Music Concourse, affirming that the ramp would have no significant effect on the environment.

The Fine Arts Museums described to the Recreation and Park Commission a major renovation of the de Young Museum inside the existing building: new American art galleries, conservation laboratories for paintings, tapestries and decorative arts, more storage and a restaurant where the art school then was; Adolph Rosekrans, the museums' architect, showed schematic drawings.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved the Fine Arts Museums' plans, drawn by Adolph Rosekrans, for a transformer and cooling tower at the de Young Museum and an underground chiller room and cooling tower at the Legion of Honor, in preparation for the Dresden and King Tut exhibitions.

The Recreation and Park Commission approved an interim seismic shoring scheme for the de Young Museum: 14 buttresses projecting about 30 feet from the building to anchor roof bracing, on piers 15 to 45 feet deep, angled at the main entrance to keep disabled access, and expected to stand for several years.

M. H. de Young, Director-General of the Midwinter Fair, formally handed the fair's Art Building and its annex, with their collections, to the Park Commissioners as the Memorial Museum, before nearly 3,000 people.
A new annex to the Memorial Museum, begun in the winter of 1895, was finished, divided into eight halls.
The museum building was repaired after the 1906 earthquake, for $9,958.50.

Under Charter Amendment No. 29, the Board of Park Commissioners conveyed the M. H. de Young Memorial Museum building, its contents and its grounds in Golden Gate Park, held in trust since M. H. de Young's deed to the board, to the museum's newly organized Board of Trustees.

With a large annex to the Museum finished in November 1896 and gifts still pouring in, the Park Commissioners began a second annex, 70 by 30 feet, for a new picture gallery, and built a furnace and engine room to heat the whole building against damp and mildew.

M. H. de Young submitted plans for a new Memorial Museum to the Park Commission on September 1, 1916; they were accepted, the cornerstone was laid on April 15, 1917, and building of the first unit began at once.

Before ten thousand people the new museum was dedicated on January 2, 1921, after de Young handed the Park Commission the deed of trust placing it and its contents in the commissioners' keeping as a museum free to the people forever; he gave it on the one condition that it never be closed and never charge admission.
The Board of Park Commissioners gratefully accepted M. H. de Young's offer to build at his own expense, and give the city, an extension of the M. H. de Young Memorial Museum.

The Fine Arts Museums' trustees authorized change orders of up to $265,000 in all on Christensen & Foster's contract for the de Young renovation project, for which the museums had committed bequest and foundation money in May 1976.

Edward Larrabee Barnes presented his master plan for the de Young, in four phases from the front of the building to the space the Asian Art Museum then held, at an estimated $75 million, about $25 million of it for seismic strengthening; the trustees approved it as Resolution 56.
The Fine Arts Museums' trustees chose the Swiss firm Herzog & de Meuron to draw a conceptual plan for a new de Young; it was presented to the board on June 10, 1999.
The Fine Arts Museums' executive committee recommended that Herzog & de Meuron, with Fong & Chan Architects as the local firm, go on to design and engineer the new de Young.

Pierre de Meuron presented the schematic drawings for the new de Young to the Fine Arts Museums' trustees: a building set on the Music Concourse across from the Academy of Sciences, with an education tower at its northeast corner open free to the public.

The Fine Arts Museums' executive committee approved the schematic design of the new de Young and adopted its environmental findings, a week after the Planning and Recreation and Park Commissions certified the project's environmental impact report.
The old de Young building closed to the public on December 31, 2000, after 100,000 people visited it that December, so that it could be emptied for the new museum.
The Fine Arts Museums' trustees approved the next stage of design development of Herzog & de Meuron's plans for the new de Young, as Resolution 1371.
The old de Young buildings were demolished from March to May 2002, all but the wing the Asian Art Museum still occupied, and excavation for the new museum was to follow.
The new de Young opened on October 15, 2005, built by the general contractor Swinerton Builders over two years and ten months, with more than 1.1 million pounds of copper.

The Fine Arts Museums' trustees thanked Herzog & de Meuron for the design of the new de Young, with its perforated copper skin and its education tower turned to the street grid of the Richmond and Sunset, and Fong & Chan Architects, its principal architects, who produced the construction documents.

The Fine Arts Museums' trustees thanked Hood Design, Walter Hood's firm, chosen in 1999 for the new de Young's landscape: more than five acres of new grounds and 344 trees, keeping the old museum's sphinxes, the Pool of Enchantment and twenty-one century-old palms.
